extracted.intended_audience: computer-science students and authors of technical term papers/lecture notes (students in a CS writing/editing class)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for writing and copy-editing technical prose (term papers, lecture notes, expository CS writing), emphasising clarity, punctuation, style, and use of tooling. Includes both manual editing rules and how to interpret automated readability/diction tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crowding the page with too many symbols / avoid reusing primed notation
rubrics_metrics.description: It's just not elegant to have too many symbols crowded on the page; you are going to get into trouble when you start also using the construct Hj (that is, Hi primed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either write 'each Hi is ...' or invent another name for the concept if it will be used repeatedly. Avoid confusing reuse of primed versions of symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apostrophe for genitive (possessive) case
rubrics_metrics.description: You do need an apostrophe for the genitive (possessive) case; 'Hi S descendants' doesn't work at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'Hi's descendants' rather than omitting the apostrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of 'the one vertex path', write 'the one-vertex path'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphenation prevents misreading of compound modifiers; apply when a multiword adjective modifies a noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct prepositions for technical phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The preposition 'at' would be better than 'of' in 'vertex of distance d'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose prepositions that reflect mathematical/technical conventions to avoid awkward phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave spacing around inline references
rubrics_metrics.description: We certainly need a space here: 'using 4.3 (below) we derive ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper spacing so references and surrounding text don't run together and become hard to parse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect logical ordering of lemmas/theorems and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors have a disconcerting habit of using a lemma or theorem that is not proved until later on in the book; this can leave the reader wondering whether someone hasn't pulled a fast one on him (essentially by using a result to prove that same result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it clear to the reader that proof structures respect the necessary ordering — don't rely on results that are proved only later without clear forward references or justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties / non-breaking spaces to prevent harmful line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Using ties: TeX and other systems allow you to specify that certain blanks are not to be used as line breaks (e.g., put ties after the word 'dominates' in the phrase 'v dominates x and x dominates w'). In 'if e is ...' it is best to put such a tie between e and 'is'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep line breaks from interrupting or distorting the message by non-breaking spaces/ties in critical short constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous word-sense coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of the unfortunate coincidence! Sometimes we cannot use an idiom because some word is also being used in another sense (e.g., 'left' as direction vs past tense). 'The node T is left' might be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose wording that avoids homonym-induced ambiguities, especially when two different senses occur in the same context (e.g., aerodynamics + complex planes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sequences of examples that build on one another
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of examples that build upon one another is much more useful than a number of unrelated ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise examples pedagogically so each example extends or clarifies the previous ones; the Haddad and Schiffer paper is cited as an example of good sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which vs. that (restrictive vs. non-restrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That' is the defining or restrictive pronoun, 'which' the non-defining or non-restrictive. If you can substitute 'that' for 'which', do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule for everyday, expository 'shirtsleeve' prose (not necessarily literary prose). Fowler and Strunk & White discussion cited; Mary-Claire's practical rule attributed to Leslie Lamport: if replacing 'which' by 'that' sounds all right, make the substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply 'which/that' guidance mindful of genre and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Mary-Claire said the rules hold for everyday expository prose, not literary prose; tone consists entirely of making tiny choices like which vs that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide when to violate everyday rules knowingly (literary effect). Small choices accumulate and affect readership and attention; many readers are indoctrinated by Strunk & White's prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use readability indices as coarse signals, not absolute truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Readability routines produce 'grade' levels based on average words per sentence and average syllables per word; authors of each index fit a plane by regression to samples labelled by eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to minimise grade level moderately (Don's usual aim) but don't overdo it — the metrics are superficial and can miss musical or domain-appropriate long sentences (e.g., Church). Use them as prompts to re-read, not as definitive judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret style-tool diagnostics beyond the headline grade
rubrics_metrics.description: Style programs output other parameters: average sentence length, percentage of sentences much shorter/longer than average, percentage of sentences beginning with various parts of speech, classification of sentence types and their frequencies, percentages of nouns/adjectives/verbs, passive voice counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these statistics to understand composition patterns (e.g., lots of passive voice in technical work). Note program heuristics: a sentence is considered 'passive' if a passive verb appears anywhere; any sentence that begins 'It...' or 'There...' may be classed as 'expletive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical about style-tool judgments that don't fit domain usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction program flags words/phrases it deems 'questionable' (e.g., 'gratuitous', 'number of', 'due to') and suggests alternatives; but some flagged usages are appropriate in mathematics ('due to Cauchy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human judgment to accept/reject suggestions; Don reports changing some automated edits back (e.g., 'owing to' vs 'due to'). About half of diction's suggestions are accepted in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary words and tighten phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sentences could be improved by cutting them shorter; whole phrases can often be dropped without loss of meaning ('he has heard' can be reduced). A hallmark of good writing is that it answers more questions than it raises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise alternatives ('We remove the spaces because...' instead of 'The reason for removing the spaces from the list is that ...'). Strive for clarity, coherence, accuracy, and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer periods over semicolons; avoid overlong sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write one long sentence if you can say the same thing in two short ones. A semicolon should be used only where the separated clauses have a very close relationship; semicolons can slow the pace and convey '19th-century mustiness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break up long sentences; use semicolons sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition / overuse of filler words
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent repetition of a word like 'this', 'they', 'just', or 'then' is common; reading the piece aloud will help you spot such over-uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit to remove repeated function words and filler; vary phrasing for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms and informal phrasings in technical prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of sentences that begin 'Anyway,...', descriptions like 'pretty straightforward', or awkward phrases like 'again iterate through'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more formal, precise wording in technical writing; conversational idioms can sound unprofessional or unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject near the beginning; prefer subject-verb-object order
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sentences suffer from having their subject and verb separated by many words—these are hard to read. Sticking to subject-verb-object style reduces such problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place subject and verb close together, avoid lengthy intervening clauses; this also reduces overuse of passive constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The style program flags passive voice (counted if a passive verb appears anywhere); over-use of passive voice makes prose less direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active constructions in expository writing unless passive is justified for focus or formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rhetorical/creative exercises as training, not ends in themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse-writing and other 'calisthenics' are useful exercises but are 'really only exercises'; some exercises (e.g., writing out every rhetorical term in Lanham) may not be profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose practice activities that demonstrably improve your prose; don’t assume all 'clever' exercises yield usable gains.
